title: While the World Pushes Immigrants Away, Spain Invites Half a Million
dek: Pedro Sánchez is Defying Global Political Trends, and it is Working
author: Yann Grechez Elkoubi
body:
In January, Spain’s governing coalition announced they had passed a motion to regularize over 500,000 undocumented migrants. The rules are simple: if you have spent 5 uninterrupted months in Spain before 2026, you do not have a criminal record, and you do not currently hold any administrative status, you are allowed to obtain a legal residency and work authorization permit.

However, the response to this policy has not been similarly simple. A wide variety of political actors, ranging from Spain’s conservative opposition to the White House, have expressed complete outrage over this policy. Figures like Elon Musk even called the policy an act of “high treason” towards the Spanish people. Why has a domestic law of a middle power like Spain flooded news outlets across the entire globe? What are the economic and social implications of this mass regularization? Does Pedro Sánchez benefit politically from swimming against the right-wing populist tide currently sweeping international politics? Let's dive in.

The Case for Regularization

The justification for this policy was twofold: a social dimension concerning the basic rights of undocumented persons, and an economic one, in reference to the labor shortage Spain is currently experiencing. Socially, undocumented migrants in Spain have long dealt with labor exploitation, especially in the agricultural sector. Those who can safely complete the journey from their home countries and find a job often encounter deplorable working conditions, experiencing long hours under scorching heat and unsanitary conditions, and are paid far below minimum wage. Labor rights that are supposed to defend people against this kind of exploitation fail to apply to undocumented individuals, simply because the law doesn’t protect those who are not registered under it. 

Studies have already shown that heat-related hospitalizations for workers have declined in provinces with greater exposure to the mass regularization policy. Under this view, mass regularization provides visibility to previously invisible people, and affords them the rights and dignity every worker in Spain usually enjoys. 

Economically, Spain’s low birth rates and an ageing population (with an exceptionally high life expectancy) are putting the country at what Sánchez calls “a demographic crossroads”: not enough active workers in the labor market to sustain the country’s welfare state (pensions, healthcare, public services). Elma Saiz, Sánchez’s migration minister, stated that Spain must register 250,000 foreign workers per year in order to sustain the welfare state, justifying this mass regularization program, which intends to provide documents to 300,000 migrants per year for the next three years. Regularization brings people out of the informal economy and allows them to work legally, paying taxes and contributing to social security, safeguarding Spain’s welfare system. 

Spanish workers themselves cannot fill in these positions because much of Spain’s unemployment is structural: unemployed Spanish workers are not able or willing to work where labor is most needed. Many labor shortages concentrate in sectors like agriculture, elder-care, domestic work, and construction, which are usually quite physically demanding, seasonal, and poorly-paid. The statistics clearly reflect this, where migrants make up 71% of domestic service workers, 45% of hospitality workers, 32% of construction workers, and 31% of agricultural workers. 

Why Critics See Regularization as a Threat

Sánchez’s opposition and the broader global conservative movement have responded with intense indignation. A strong argument has stemmed from the “great replacement theory”, which suggests that programs like these create pull factors to encourage more migration, which will eventually supplant the Spanish identity and social fabric. “We cannot take in even one more; we are not prepared, and some of us also simply do not want to. There are entire neighborhoods that remind you that you are in the Maghreb or in Quito.”, claims the Vox representative in the Catalan parliament.

Opposition members have also argued that this policy violates Spanish rule of law not only because of what it encourages, but also because of how it was passed. Critics argue this program encourages and rewards illegality, as granting undocumented migrants a legal status motivates more potential migrants to come into Spain illegally, and undermines the credibility of the existing regular migration pathways. Moreover, this policy was passed through a royal decree, a legal instrument in Spain that allows policies to take effect immediately in cases of “extraordinary and urgent necessity”. Sánchez argued this policy addressed an urgent humanitarian and economic necessity, as hundreds of thousands of workers were currently employed without full legal protection. Opposition members argued that this regularization should have undergone the usual debate, scrutiny, and negotiations, with critics describing this as a flagrant violation of the rule of law and democratic principles.

Sánchez’s Gamble Against the Global Right

Overall, the mass regularization program has become one of Sánchez’s most controversial political moves in his 8 years of leadership. While advocates champion the safeguarding of human rights and Spanish economic welfare, opponents believe this policy threatens to saturate public services, replace Spanish identity, and undermine the rule of law. Long queues are already forming in front of administration buildings in Spain, and time will only tell the true effect this mass regularization will have on Spanish society.

Sánchez implemented this program just months before bidding for reelection, a political Hail Mary. Instead of mimicking the rhetoric of right-wing populism and assimilating their policies, as many incumbent leaders in Europe who face electoral threats from their right-wing opposition have done, Sánchez went full force in the opposite direction. This policy not only presents a clear clash against the Trump-era deportation politics, but also against the wider right-wing nationalist ideology sweeping over Western democracies.

Sánchez’s firm opposition to Trump and right-wing populism, not only in the issue of immigration but also on that of renewable energy, international law, and defence spending, has given his party what some call a political lifeline, turning him into the face of progressive politics worldwide. Recent polls estimate that Sánchez’s party will receive its highest voter share since the July 2023 elections, at 36.4%, 4.6 points higher than this last March. Whether this strategy will translate into lasting political strength remains uncertain, but for now, Sánchez has turned migration from a political liability into a defining symbol of his broader ideological campaign against global right-wing populism, and it is working.
